target_customer: Architects, engineers, contractors and building product manufacturers
problem: Building codes are scattered, hard to search and vary by jurisdiction, so professionals lose time and risk non-compliant designs.
business_model: Freemium SaaS with paid pro subscriptions plus advertising and marketing services for building product manufacturers
product_category: Building code search and compliance software

founders.name: Scott Reynolds
founders.background_notes: Worked as an architect and left to build UpCodes per TechCrunch 2018-06.

founders.name: Garrett Reynolds
founders.background_notes: Scott's brother and former PlanGrid software engineer per TechCrunch 2018-06 and the YC page.

technical_complexity.rationale: Parsing and normalizing code adoptions across many jurisdictions needs NLP and heavy data work, but the core product was a searchable library.

defensibility.rationale: A large cleaned code library and user base help, but the underlying codes are public law and the ICC sued over copyright use.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: The ICC sued UpCodes over copyright, and Scott Reynolds' profile says a judge later ruled for fair use; no incumbent bought it.

market_need_then: Architects and engineers needed to look up locally adopted codes that were often in clunky PDFs or paywalled; the founder's own frustration as an architect drove the idea.

branding.domain_note: Uses up.codes, a domain hack, not the exact .com.
branding.community_and_virality: About 800,000 monthly users per the YC page, mostly via product-led growth and the public legal fight with the ICC.

brand_strength.rationale: Known in architecture and construction circles, with press coverage, but no sourced evidence of brand-driven growth.

outcome_analysis: UpCodes built a free searchable code library that grew to hundreds of thousands of monthly users, backed by founders with architecture and PlanGrid experience. It raised small rounds, 785K by mid 2018, 3.36M in 2021 and a 3.5M Series A in 2023, so it stayed capital efficient but also modest in scale. It survived a copyright suit by the ICC and has shifted toward AI tools, Copilot and a specifications workflow, and remains active.
